content:
I have been using Claude to work through the exercises and I have been generally very impressed with its performance. Basically not a single exercise need my intervention, and I am the slow part of the process, because I try to read and understand the proofs.

But it just dawned on me, Claude is so good at writing Lean for Real Analysis because surely a lot of these sorries are already in mathlib. So I sent it on a bit of exploration to analyze the overlap with mathlib.

Note: I have done zero checking whether any of this is actually correct, but also have no reason to doubt it greatly.

Here is Claude's own exec summary

Mathlib Coverage of Tao's Analysis I Exercises

I systematically checked all 730 sorry-marked exercises in the Lean 4 companion to Tao's "Analysis I" against Mathlib (searching the actual source on disk, not vibes).

Results:

- 16% directly in Mathlib — solvable by calling a named Mathlib lemma (closure of intervals, derivative rules, Schröder-Bernstein, Zorn's lemma, IVT, L'Hôpital, etc.)
- 49% math is in Mathlib but types differ — the theorem exists in Mathlib for standard types (ℝ, ℤ, Filter.Tendsto, HasSum), but the exercise uses custom types (custom Nat, custom Real, custom Sequence,
custom Series, custom Partition/Integral). The AI knows what to prove but must reconstruct the proof against a different API.

- 35% not in Mathlib at all — counterexample constructions, decidability puzzles, custom framework exercises (Riemann-Stieltjes integration, Jordan measure), bridge lemmas between type systems, and a few
genuinely unformalized results (Riemann rearrangement theorem, ratio/root test internals).

Takeaway for AI evaluation: Only 16% of exercises could be "cheated" by memorizing Mathlib. For the remaining 84%, the AI must either translate known math to unfamiliar types (49%) or solve something with
no known formalized answer (35%). The hardest chapters are Ch 11 (Riemann integration — 72% not in Mathlib, entirely custom framework) and Measure Theory (custom Jordan/Lebesgue definitions). The easiest is
Ch 10 (differentiation — 60% directly in Mathlib, uses Mathlib's own HasDerivWithinAt types).

Full report with per-exercise tables: https://github.com/rkirov/analysis/blob/mathlib-coverage-analysis/mathlib_coverage_analysis.md

So still a lot of reason to be impressed, and now I wonder whether I should be attempting to upstream some to mathlib. Undoubtedly I will learn a lot through the review process, but from what I gather I better get reviewer's time precommited and preinterested. Will explore this more after I finish the full book formalization (roughly 3 chapters remaining).
